A pool is a contract holding two tokens; a trade is a call to it that takes some of one and leaves some of the other, priced by a formula that depends only on what the pool currently holds. Anyone can create a pool for any pair, so the catalogue is permissionless and the quality varies enormously.
## Atomic settlement

The whole swap — possibly across several pools — succeeds or fails as a unit, inside one transaction. This is the central advantage over any cross-chain design: there is no window in which you hold a half-finished trade, and the minimum output you specify is enforced by the contract itself rather than promised.
## Fee tiers and depth

The same pair can have several pools with different fee levels. A stable pair can be served well by a very low fee, while a volatile pair needs a higher one to pay the people providing liquidity for the risk they take. A router picks a path across pools; the headline rate alone doesn't say which is cheapest, because a lower fee on a thin pool can cost more in price impact than a higher fee on a deep one.
## Approvals

Moving an existing token requires giving a contract permission to do so first, which is a separate transaction. It is worth knowing this is an allowance rather than a one-off: it stays until changed, which is both a convenience and something worth keeping an eye on.
## What a swap costs
• Ethereum's own fee for the transaction, which dominates for small trades.
• The pool's fee, a fixed share of the amount traded.
• Price impact, which depends on your size against the pool's depth.
• A separate Ethereum fee for an approval, when one is needed.
complex: ## Constant product and its descendants
The original rule keeps the product of reserves fixed across a trade:
`x · y = k`

An input Δx returns Δy = y·Δx/(x+Δx) before fees. The marginal price is y/x and the realised price is always worse, with the gap growing as Δx/x — this is price impact, and it is a property of the formula, not a charge by anyone. Liquidity under this rule is spread over every price from zero to infinity, most of which will never trade, so capital efficiency is poor.
## Concentrated liquidity

Later designs let a provider choose a price range and supply liquidity only inside it, behaving within that range like a constant-product pool holding much larger virtual reserves. Capital efficiency improves by orders of magnitude for a pair that stays in range, and the provider is left holding only one of the two assets when it leaves. Aggregate depth therefore becomes a function of price — a pool can be very deep at the current price and thin a few percent away, which is invisible in any single quoted rate.
## Impermanent loss as a cost of providing

A provider's holding is rebalanced continuously against the market by the traders themselves, so it ends up with more of whichever asset fell. Against simply holding the two assets, the shortfall for a constant-product pool at a price ratio r is
which is zero when the price returns and grows either side of it. Fee income has to exceed this for providing to be worthwhile, which is why fee tiers track volatility.
## Ordering and extractable value

Because trades settle in a public ordered sequence, whoever decides the order can profit from knowing a trade before it executes: placing one in front and one behind it captures the price it moves. The minimum-output bound is the user's defence, and it converts a worse price into a failed transaction rather than preventing the extraction. Private transaction routing avoids the public queue, at the cost of relying on whoever carries it to include it at all — a dropped transaction is the characteristic failure of that approach, and the reason it must be detected rather than waited on indefinitely.
## Path selection

Finding the best execution is an optimisation over paths and splits, not a lookup: a large trade may be best served split across several pools and several hops, since impact is superlinear in size within each. The comparison that matters is always the output after all fees and impact, which is why two routers quoting the same pair can honestly differ.

tutorials.title: Swaps in more than one step
tutorials.summary: Why a swap through other coins isn't guaranteed, and how padding helps.

simple: Some coins can't be swapped straight into each other. Then the swap goes through a coin in between: for example USDC into DOGE, then DOGE into BNB.
Each step is its own trade, made a few minutes after the one before. Prices keep moving in between, so the last step can cost more than it did when you checked.
If it costs too much, that step stops. Nothing is lost: the coin in between stays in your wallet, and you can finish the swap later.
## Padding
Padding gives the later steps room for the price to move. Each step of padding adds 0.5%.
• Paying someone a set amount, padding buys a little more of the coin in between. They still get exactly what you typed, and what isn't needed stays in your wallet.
• Swapping for yourself, padding lets the later steps accept a slightly worse price instead of stopping.
More padding makes the swap more likely to finish. It can't make it certain: a big enough price move, or a network that pauses, can still stop a step.
detailed: ## Why there's no direct swap

Each exchange network only trades the coins it holds pools or market makers for. When no single network trades both coins, the swap goes through a coin that two of them share, and each step is a separate trade on its own network.
## Why a later step can stop

A step only starts once the coin from the step before has arrived, which can take minutes. The price for the next step is fixed only when that step is sent, and the exchange then pays out only if it can still meet the least the step was allowed to pay. If the market moved past that, the exchange refunds the step instead of filling it at a worse price.
## What padding changes

Padding widens that allowance. When the last step pays a set amount to someone, it buys more of the coin in between up front, so the last step can still afford that amount after a move. When it doesn't, it lowers the least each later step will accept.
Neither changes what the exchanges do. They are still independent trades that can each fail, which is why a multi-step swap is never guaranteed.
complex: ## Sequential execution risk

A route of n trades executed one after another is exposed to price movement over the whole time between the first quote and the last fill. With each step's price roughly a random walk, the spread of outcomes grows with the square root of that time, so a route whose steps take minutes each carries noticeably more risk than one trade.
## Slippage limits as a guarantee

Each step carries a minimum output. The exchange fills the step only if it can deliver at least that, and refunds the input otherwise. That makes every step all-or-nothing on its own, but it makes the route as a whole conditional: the probability that it finishes is the product of each step's probability of clearing its limit.
## The effect of padding

Loosening a step's limit by a fraction p raises the chance that it clears. Overbuying the intermediate asset by p, when the final output is fixed, does the same from the other side: the final step needs less than it holds. Either way the gain shows up in the tail, against moves larger than the limit would otherwise allow, and it never reaches certainty, because the size of a move is unbounded.

tutorials.title: Recovery shares from friends and family
tutorials.summary: Split your backup among people you trust, so a few of them together can bring your wallet back.

simple: Your recovery phrase is the key to your whole wallet. If you lose it, your money is gone. Secret sharing gives you a safety net.
You can cut your phrase into pieces, called shares, and give one to each person you trust. It's like a treasure map torn into pieces: one piece on its own shows nothing.
You choose how many pieces are needed. For example, 7 people, and any 4 of them together can bring your wallet back if you lose it, or for your family if you pass away.

Set it up in Profile → Backup & security → Secret sharing, and send each share as a private Zcash message to a contact, by email with a password, or as words in a letter. To use shares later, choose Recover with shares on Kalda's welcome screen.
Choose people who won't all get together behind your back: enough of them together could open your wallet. If you think too many shares are no longer safe, move your money to a new wallet.
detailed: Secret sharing is built on a well-known idea from cryptography, Shamir's secret sharing, published by Adi Shamir in 1979. Kalda's shares follow SLIP-39, a public, open standard that turns Shamir shares into lists of words.
• Threshold: you pick N people and a number T. Any T shares rebuild the recovery phrase; T − 1 or fewer reveal nothing about it, not even a hint.

• Words with error detection: each share is written with a fixed word list, so it can be copied by hand, read aloud or kept on paper, and carries a checksum, so a mistyped word is caught instead of producing the wrong wallet.
• Sets stay together: every share in a set carries the same identifier, so shares from two different sets can't be mixed by accident.
## Getting shares to people safely

A private Zcash message is encrypted by the Zcash network itself, so only the recipient can read it. Email and chat apps aren't private, so a share sent that way travels locked with a password; give the password another way, such as in person, by phone or in your will. Words in a letter need nothing more.

No scheme can take shares back once they are given out: making a new set doesn't stop the old one working. And if more than N − T people lose their shares, there aren't enough left to recover. The only way to retire old shares is to move your money to a new wallet.
complex: Shamir's secret sharing rests on a simple fact about polynomials: two points fix a straight line, three points fix a parabola, and in general T points fix exactly one polynomial of degree T − 1.
## Splitting
To share a secret s with threshold T, choose a random polynomial of degree T − 1 whose value at zero is the secret. Each person receives one point on that curve, taken at a different, non-zero x.
`f(x) = s + a₁x + a₂x² + … + a₍T−1₎x^(T−1)     share i = (xᵢ, f(xᵢ))`
## Rebuilding
Any T shares determine the polynomial uniquely, and Lagrange interpolation gives its value at zero, which is the secret:
`s = f(0) = Σᵢ yᵢ · Πⱼ≠ᵢ xⱼ / (xⱼ − xᵢ)`
## Why fewer shares reveal nothing

The arithmetic is done in a finite field (for byte-sized secrets, typically a field of 256 elements), not with ordinary numbers. With only T − 1 points, every possible secret is matched by exactly one polynomial through those points, so each value is equally likely. This is information-theoretic security: it holds no matter how much computing power an attacker has.

In practice, long secrets are split byte by byte with fresh random coefficients each time. Plain Shamir can't tell a wrong share from a right one, so practical schemes add a checksum to each share and a digest of the secret to detect mistakes. And the scheme protects the secret only until T holders combine their shares, so the threshold is a trade-off: high enough to resist collusion, low enough to survive lost shares.

tutorials.title: Your account type
tutorials.summary: Choose how Kalda is organised, which coins appear on your wallet, and your language.

simple: When you first open Kalda, it asks for your account type: Personal, Business, Investment, Trading or Developer. Pick one. Each organises Kalda around what you do: the features that go with it are to hand, and the rest stay out of your way.

Switching type changes nothing under the hood: your coins, balances and addresses stay exactly as they are; only the organisation and layout change. Money sent to you always arrives, whatever you chose. You can change it any time on your Profile.
Profile → Coins on my wallet lets you choose which coins appear on your wallet screen. Hiding a coin never touches the money in it.
The app's language is in Profile → Settings.
detailed: What each type brings to the front:
• Personal account: a short guide the first time you open each main page, tips on the trickier actions and, on its own, a handful of popular coins (plus any coin you already hold).
• Business account: XRP tools, such as shared wallets with co-signers, locks and scheduled payments.
• Developer account: everything, plus Developer Settings and the developer docs.

• Investment account: everything the Trading account shows, plus staking on each coin's page where the coin offers it, and interest on USDC and USDT through lending. Each one lists its risks before anything is sent.

• Trading account: Kalda first explains honestly that most people who trade often lose money, and that a centralised exchange usually costs less for frequent trading. After that, Swap shows a price check against the wider market, and when a swap goes through another coin on the way, the path it takes.

Every type is private: payments to you go to private addresses, and Kalda spends private money on its own. Encrypted messages are for everyone, whatever your type. If something arrives that your type doesn't show yet, Kalda tells you what it is and offers to turn it on, so nothing you own stays hidden.
## Why it works this way
Grouping features by what people do, rather than by skill, makes them easier to find: you pick the tasks you care about, and everything else stays out of the way.
complex: ## Progressive disclosure

Progressive disclosure is a long-standing principle of interface design: present the few options most people need, and defer advanced ones until they're asked for. It reduces cognitive load, the mental effort needed to understand a screen, and with it the chance of mistakes.

Research on personalised interfaces finds that letting people choose what they see (an adaptable interface) works better than an app that rearranges itself, and that grouping features by task works better than grouping them by expertise.
## Self-custody

In a self-custody wallet, whoever holds the private keys controls the funds. There's no bank to call, no password reset and no chargeback: a confirmed blockchain transaction is final, and a lost recovery phrase can't be recovered by anyone else.
## Separating view from behaviour

A good layered design changes presentation only. The same keys, addresses and balances exist whatever is ticked, so changing your choice never moves money or changes what other people can send you; it only changes how much of it you see.

tutorials.title: Notifications
tutorials.summary: What Kalda tells you about, made on your own phone.

simple: Kalda can let you know on your phone when something happens, such as:
• A swap finishing or being refunded, or a move between your private and public Zcash balances finishing.
• A new secret message (who it's from, never what it says), or a wallet skin someone has sent you.
• XRP locked for you, arriving, going out on schedule or coming back.

These notifications are made on your phone. No company sends them, and Kalda has no server of its own that knows about you. Kalda asks for permission the first time one would be useful, and you can turn them off in your phone's settings.
detailed: Most apps rely on a push service: the app maker's server sends a message to your phone through Apple or Google. Kalda's notifications are local instead: your phone looks at public networks directly and shows the notification itself. That works because:
• Public blockchains can be read by anyone, so your phone can see when a payment has arrived or a transaction has settled without asking anyone's permission.
• Cross-chain swap networks publish the status of every swap, so the outcome of a swap (paid out or refunded) can be looked up openly.
• The XRP Ledger keeps escrows (locks) as public records, showing who will receive what and when.
• Zcash shielded messages are encrypted to the recipient, so only your own wallet can discover and read them.
## What to expect

Your phone's operating system decides when apps may run in the background, to save battery, so a notification can arrive a little after the event itself. Private Zcash messages are found while Kalda is open, because only your wallet can decrypt them.
complex: ## Push and pull

There are two ways to learn about events. In a push model, a server watches for events and sends them to a device. In a pull model, the device asks the source itself. Push saves the device work; pull avoids relying on, and revealing yourself to, a middleman.

A push notification needs a device token registered with the platform's notification service and with the app's server. That pairing links one device to its activity, so whoever runs the server learns what the user cares about and when. A pull model keeps that knowledge on the device.
## Reading public state

Blockchains are replicated public ledgers. Any client can ask a node for an account's balance, a transaction's status or a ledger object, much as anyone can read a public notice board. Light clients go further and check what they're told against block headers instead of trusting the server.
## Finding private payments

In shielded systems such as Zcash, outputs are encrypted to the recipient's key. A wallet discovers its own payments by trial decryption: it tries to decrypt each new output with its viewing key, and only outputs meant for it succeed. Nobody else can tell which outputs belong to whom, which is why this scanning has to happen on the recipient's own device.
## Settled, not just sent

A transaction is final once the network's consensus can no longer reverse it. In proof-of-work chains finality is probabilistic and grows with each confirmation; in chains such as the XRP Ledger, a validated ledger is final within seconds. A trustworthy "complete" notification waits for that point.

tutorials.title: Network fees
tutorials.summary: The small charge each network takes to carry a payment.

simple: Every time you send crypto, the network that carries it charges a small fee. It's like postage on a letter: you pay it to get your payment delivered.
The network fee goes to the network, not to Kalda. You see it before you send, and it's taken from your balance.
Some coins need a little to stay behind. For example, an XRP wallet must always keep a small amount. If you tap the most you can send, room is left for the fee and anything that has to stay.
Sending a token such as USDC on Ethereum needs a little ETH for its fee. A swap also has the swap network's own fee, shown on its own line on the Swap screen.
detailed: Each network sets its own fee rules, and they're all public:

• Bitcoin, Litecoin, Dogecoin and Bitcoin Cash: the fee depends on the payment's size in bytes, not on the amount. A payment that gathers many small coins is bigger, so it costs more. When the network is busy, fees rise.

• Ethereum, BNB Chain and Avalanche: the fee is called gas. Ethereum's fee market (EIP-1559) has a base fee that rises and falls with demand, plus a small tip. Tokens such as USDC and USDT pay their gas in ETH.
• XRP Ledger: a tiny fee, plus a reserve that must stay in every account, and a little more for each thing the account holds on the ledger, such as a trust line or an escrow.
• Zcash: fees follow ZIP 317, based on how many pieces a payment has, not on the amount.
• Solana: a small fixed fee per signature. An account must be emptied completely or keep a small minimum balance.
• TRON: often free, paid from daily bandwidth; sending to a brand-new address costs a little extra to create it.
• Cardano, Cosmos and RUNE: Cardano charges by transaction size and asks every output to carry a minimum of ADA; Cosmos and RUNE charge a fee set by their networks.
complex: ## Why fees exist

Block space is scarce: each block can hold only so much. Fees ration that space and make spam expensive. They're paid to the miners or validators who include transactions, or in some designs destroyed (burned), which makes the remaining coins slightly scarcer. Moving a million costs the network the same as moving one, since the work is checking signatures and storing data, not counting value; that's why fees follow size or computation, unlike card fees, which follow the amount.
## UTXO and account models

Bitcoin-style chains use unspent transaction outputs (UTXOs): coins are discrete pieces, and a payment spends whole pieces as inputs and creates new outputs, including change back to the sender. Size, and so the fee, grows with the number of inputs and outputs. Account-based chains such as Ethereum keep a balance per account, and fees depend on the computation a transaction needs.
`fee = fee rate × transaction size        size ≈ overhead + per-input + per-output`
## Fee markets

When demand exceeds space, users compete by offering higher fees, like an auction. Ethereum's EIP-1559 makes this more predictable: a base fee adjusts automatically from block to block depending on how full the last block was, and is burned, while a smaller priority fee goes to the validator.
`fee paid = gas used × (base fee + priority fee)     base fee moves by at most 12.5% per block`
## Reserves and dust

Some ledgers charge for storage rather than computation: every account or object takes up space on every node, so a minimum balance (a reserve, or Solana's rent-exempt minimum) must stay locked while it exists. Tiny outputs that would cost more to spend than they're worth are called dust, and many networks refuse to create them.

tutorials.title: Gas, and how to pay less for it
tutorials.summary: Why your dollars need a little gas to move, and how to keep that cost low.

simple: Digital dollars such as USDC and USDT live on networks like Ethereum, Polygon and BNB Chain. To move them, the network charges a small fee called gas, and it has to be paid in that network's own coin: ETH on Ethereum, POL on Polygon, BNB on BNB Chain.
So holding dollars isn't quite enough: each place your dollars sit needs a little gas before they can move.
## How to pay less
• Buy gas once, not every time. Every purchase has its own small cost, so buying enough for several payments at once is cheaper than buying a tiny bit before each one.
• Keep your dollars on the cheaper networks. Moving dollars on Polygon or BNB Chain usually costs a fraction of a cent. On Ethereum it can cost much more, especially when the network is busy.
• Fewer, bigger payments cost less than many small ones, since each payment pays its own gas whatever the amount.
• When someone pays you, ask them to use a cheap network if they can.
Gas goes to the network that carries your payment, not to Kalda.
detailed: USDC and USDT are tokens: entries kept by a program (a smart contract) on each network. Moving a token means asking that program to update its records, and every network charges for the work in its own coin, known as gas.
• Ethereum: gas is paid in ETH. Its price follows demand and can rise sharply when the network is busy.
• Polygon: gas is paid in POL, usually a tiny fraction of a cent per transfer.
• BNB Chain: gas is paid in BNB, usually under a cent per transfer.
• Solana: fees are paid in SOL and are tiny, but receiving a token for the first time needs a small deposit (rent) for the account that holds it.
## Private addresses

When you're paid privately, each payment arrives at a brand-new one-time address (the ERC-5564 standard for stealth addresses). That keeps payments from being linked together, but each of those addresses needs its own gas before its dollars can move.
## Ways to save
• Buy gas in one go and share it out, rather than in many small purchases: every purchase and every transfer has its own fixed cost.
• Hold and receive dollars on Polygon or BNB Chain when you can; the same dollars cost far less to move there than on Ethereum.
• Swapping dollars from one network to another costs a little too, so it's best to keep them where moving them is cheapest.
complex: ## Gas as a unit of work

On Ethereum-style networks every operation has a fixed cost in gas units, and the fee is those units times the price per unit at the time. A token transfer calls the token contract's transfer function, which updates two balances in storage and emits an event; that costs a few tens of thousands of gas units whatever the amount moved.
`fee = gas used × (base fee + priority fee)`
## Why networks differ

Ethereum's base fee is set by an EIP-1559 fee market: it rises when blocks are full and falls when they aren't, so the same transfer can cost a few cents one hour and much more the next. Polygon and BNB Chain run the same virtual machine with more block space and cheaper native coins, so the same transfer costs far less.
## Who pays

A transaction must be signed by the account it spends from, and that account pays the fee from its own native balance. A token-only account therefore can't move anything until some native coin reaches it. Account abstraction (ERC-4337) lets a separate party, a paymaster, pay the fee instead; without it, the account itself must hold gas.
## Private addresses and batching

Stealth addresses (ERC-5564) give every payment a fresh account derived from the recipient's published keys. Each such account is independent on-chain, so each must be funded with gas before it can spend. Since every transaction carries a fixed base cost (21,000 gas for a plain transfer), funding many addresses in one purchase and spreading it out costs less than a separate purchase for each.

tutorials.title: Staking and earning interest
tutorials.summary: Put coins to work for a yearly rate, and what you risk doing it.

simple: Some coins can earn a yearly rate while you hold them. On an Investment account, a coin's page shows how, when the coin offers it: Stake, and Unstake to take it back.
ETH is staked through Lido. Your ETH becomes stETH, which grows a little every day. Taking it back as ETH waits in a queue, usually a few days.
USDC and USDT earn interest through Aave. That isn't staking: your dollars are lent to borrowers, and you earn the interest they pay. You can usually take it back straight away.
Neither is a bank account. Nothing is insured, the rate isn't promised, and you could lose some or all of what you put in. Each coin's page lists the risks before anything is sent.
Every stake and unstake pays the network's fee. On a small amount, the fee can be more than a year's earnings: the screen tells you before you go ahead.
detailed: ## Staking ETH

Ethereum is secured by proof of stake: validators lock 32 ETH each and are paid for proposing and checking blocks. Lido pools ETH from many people, runs validators with it, and gives out stETH, a token that tracks your share of the pool and its rewards. The rate is Lido's average over the past week.

Getting ETH back means asking Lido's withdrawal queue. Requests are paid in order once validators have exited, so the wait depends on how many people are leaving. When it's ready, you collect it in one more step.
• Slashing: a validator that breaks the rules loses part of its stake, and with a pool that loss is shared by everyone in it.
• Contract risk: a bug or a hack in Lido's contracts could lose staked ETH.
• Price: stETH follows ETH, so its value goes up and down with ETH's.
## Lending USDC and USDT

Aave is a lending market run by smart contracts on several networks. Lenders put in a coin and receive a deposit token that grows with the interest borrowers pay. Borrowers must lock more collateral than they borrow; if it falls in value, it is sold to repay the loan.
• Rates move with demand: the more of the pool is borrowed, the more lenders earn.
• When nearly everything is borrowed, there may not be enough left to take yours back until borrowers repay or new lenders arrive.
• If collateral falls faster than it can be sold, the pool can be left short, and lenders bear it.
• The stablecoin itself can lose its $1 value, and its issuer can freeze it.
complex: ## Proof of stake

In proof of stake, the right to add blocks is given in proportion to coins locked as a bond rather than to computing work. Honest behaviour is rewarded with new coins and fees; provably dishonest behaviour, such as signing two conflicting blocks, destroys part of the bond. The yield comes from issuance and from fees paid by users.
## Liquid staking

A liquid staking token stands for a share of a staking pool. Two designs are common: a rebasing token, whose balance grows as rewards arrive, and a value-accruing token, whose balance stays fixed while each unit becomes worth more of the underlying coin. Either way, it can be traded while the stake itself stays locked, which is why its market price can drift from the coin it stands for.
## Pooled lending

A pooled lending market sets its rate by a utilisation curve: with U the share of deposits that is borrowed, the borrow rate rises slowly up to a target utilisation and steeply beyond it, to draw in lenders and push out borrowers. Lenders earn roughly the borrow rate times U, less a cut kept by the protocol.
`supply rate ≈ borrow rate × U × (1 − reserve factor)`

Loans are over-collateralised: each borrower's position has a health factor, the collateral's value times its liquidation threshold divided by the debt. Below 1, anyone may repay part of the debt and take collateral at a discount, which keeps the pool solvent as long as prices don't jump faster than liquidations can follow.
